title: GTO: Paradise Lost
label: Quick read (from summaries)
premise: In this sequel to Great Teacher Onizuka, ex-delinquent teacher Eikichi Onizuka tells fellow prison inmates how he ended up behind bars. He had become assistant homeroom teacher of a new class of high-school-age celebrities and idols, and his unorthodox efforts to protect them from rivalries, media pressure and exploitation in the entertainment industry escalated into a major incident.
life_message: A teacher who truly fights for young people, even breaking rules and paying the price himself, matters more than a system that profits from them.

content.note: Yakuza, street fighting and attempted murder in database tags; the story ends with Onizuka in prison after a 'major incident' (Wikipedia). Details to verify.
Threats against students and a psychopath character listed on MangaUpdates (to verify).

MangaDex rates it erotica; MangaUpdates lists nudity, sexual innuendo, a perverted protagonist and rape. A user review says one arc has the teacher pursuing a high-school student sexually, which it calls out of character. Framing of that arc unverified.
Seinen delinquent comedy; coarse speech likely but unconfirmed (to verify).
MangaUpdates lists attempted suicide; AniList tags bullying; students face media pressure (Wikipedia). Cap at 3 until checked (to verify).
Onizuka's rule-breaking methods are celebrated; the frame story shows they land him in prison (to verify).
Idol and showbiz industry shown exploiting young performers (Wikipedia).

Dignity vs honor.evidence: Ex-delinquent hero settles problems personally, with street fighting and yakuza clashes (MangaUpdates tags).

Order vs freedom.evidence: Onizuka's unorthodox methods override school and industry rules, landing him in prison (Wikipedia).

Civic vs kin.evidence: Loyalty is to his class of students, a chosen community rather than kin.

Equality vs hierarchy.evidence: Hero defies principals, showbiz bosses and media power on students' behalf.

Tradition vs secular-rational.evidence: Pragmatic, irreverent outlook; no religious frame.

Survival vs self-expression.evidence: Students' careers and safety weigh against their wish to be themselves.

folkways.japan: The story reflects Japanese debates over the idol industry's control of young performers and the high public expectations placed on teachers.

delivery.evidence: Summaries describe arcs of individual student crises; no source comments on speeches or preachiness (to verify).

personified.ideology: Rule-breaking, hands-on care for students over institutional procedure
Entertainment industry that profits from young talent

delivery.note: The story sides with the students against the industry, while the prison frame shows the hero's methods carry a cost.

winners_losers: Students win protection and second chances; exploitative industry figures lose; Onizuka pays with prison. Sympathy goes to the unconventional teacher, though one reviewer says a sexual-advance arc damages that sympathy.
